reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / endocrine society guidance
clinicalPearls: A life-threatening decompensation of severe hypothyroidism, typically in an elderly patient during winter, precipitated by infection, cold exposure, sedatives or non-compliance
The cardinal features are hypothermia, decreased consciousness and hypoventilation, often with hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia
Coma is frequently a misnomer, as many patients present with lethargy or confusion rather than true unconsciousness
Look for supporting signs of longstanding hypothyroidism: dry skin, non-pitting oedema, macroglossia, bradycardia, delayed reflex relaxation and a thyroidectomy scar
Diagnosis is clinical and should not await confirmatory thyroid function tests, as delay increases mortality
Coexisting adrenal insufficiency must be considered, so stress steroids are given alongside thyroid hormone replacement
Treatment combines levothyroxine and stress steroids for myxoedema coma with rewarming, ventilatory and haemodynamic support, and treatment of the precipitant
reference.pathophysiology: Myxoedema coma represents failure of physiological compensation in profound, longstanding hypothyroidism. Severe thyroid-hormone deficiency slows metabolic rate and thermogenesis, producing hypothermia, and depresses respiratory drive with carbon-dioxide retention. Reduced free-water clearance and inappropriate antidiuresis cause hyponatraemia, while impaired gluconeogenesis contributes to hypoglycaemia. Cardiovascular effects include bradycardia, reduced contractility and pericardial effusion, and mucopolysaccharide deposition in tissues produces the characteristic non-pitting oedema. A precipitating stress such as infection or sedation tips the decompensated patient into obtundation and multi-organ dysfunction.
additionalDifferentials: Hyponatraemia or hypoglycaemia of other cause
Hypercapnic respiratory failure from other causes
Stroke or other structural brain injury
additionalInvestigations: Thyroid function tests (TSH and free thyroxine) with cortisol before steroid administration
Core temperature measurement and blood glucose
Serum sodium and full electrolyte panel
Arterial blood gas to assess hypoventilation and carbon-dioxide retention
Septic screen including cultures and chest imaging to identify a precipitant
Electrocardiogram and, where indicated, echocardiography for effusion
Creatine kinase and full blood count
redFlags: Type 2 respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support
Severe hyponatraemia with seizures or worsening coma
Haemodynamic instability suggesting concurrent adrenal crisis or sepsis
reference.prognosis: Even with modern intensive care, mortality remains substantial; outcome depends on prompt recognition, early hormone replacement and treatment of the precipitating illness.
pitfalls: Delaying treatment while awaiting thyroid function results
Giving thyroid hormone without covering possible adrenal insufficiency with steroids
Aggressive active external rewarming that precipitates vasodilatory collapse
Missing the precipitating infection or sedative that triggered decompensation
references: Endocrine society guidance on severe hypothyroidism and myxoedema coma
management: Give intravenous thyroid hormone replacement (levothyroxine, with or without liothyronine) as definitive therapy without awaiting confirmatory thyroid function tests
Give empirical stress-dose glucocorticoids (hydrocortisone) alongside thyroid hormone until coexisting adrenal insufficiency is excluded
Provide supportive intensive care with airway protection and ventilatory support for hypoventilation and carbon-dioxide retention
Correct hypothermia by gradual passive rewarming and manage hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia and hypotension with cautious fluid and glucose support
Identify and treat the precipitant, particularly infection with appropriate antimicrobials, and withdraw offending sedative drugs
Monitor in critical care with cardiac monitoring for bradyarrhythmia and echocardiography for pericardial effusion
Establish maintenance oral thyroid hormone replacement on recovery and arrange endocrinology follow-up to prevent recurrence
